div.head: Ine 6.3
div.ab: Gif ðonne on gafolgildon huse oððe on gebures gefeohte, CXX scll' to wite gesylle ⁊ þæm gebure VI scll'.
Gif ðonne on gafolgeldan huse oððe on gebures gefeohte, CXX scill. to wite geselle ⁊ þam gebure VI scill.
Si autem in gauelgilda (id est in gablum reddentis) domo fiat uel in gebures, XXX sol. culpa iudicetur, et ipsi geburo VI solid.
Gif ðonne on gefolgeldan huse oððe on gebures gefeohte, CXX sciƚƚ to wite geselle ⁊ þæm gebure vi sciƚƚ.
If he should fight in the house of a renter or a farmer, let him pay 120 shillings as a fine and 6 shillings to the farmer.
If, however, he fights in the house of a taxpayer or of a gebur, he shall pay 120 shillings as a fine, and 6 shillings to the gebur.
If then he fights in the house of a rent-payer or a gebur, he is to pay 120 shillings as a fine and six shillings to the gebur.
Wenn [er] aber im Hause eines Abgabenpflichtigen oder in [dem] eines Bauern ficht, zahle er [dem König] 120 [30] Schill. zur Strafe und dem Bauern 6 Schill.
But if [he] fights in the house of a rent-paying man or in [that] of a peasant, let him pay [the king] 120 [30] shillings as a fine and the peasant 6 shillings.

note.label: cf.
note.quote: Note that §6.5 set a fine of 30 shillings for an altercation in words rather than blows

div.note: The term used is gafolgelda. On its meaning, see next note.

The gebur is called by Sir Frank Stenton “a free, but economically dependent peasant”. He received his land and stock from a lord and rendered agricultural services and other dues. If Ine’s law were meant to cover all classes of free peasant in this chapter, gafolgelda would have to be applied to the peasant who farmed land of his own; but, though Alfred 39 speaks simply of ceorl in this connection, it is not safe to assume that this was Ine’s meaning. Alfred may be improving on Ine’s ruling. Ine’s list here of compensations for fighting in houses is surely not meant to be exhaustive; the gesithcund classes are omitted, so it would not be odd if the peasant farming his own land received no mention. The law is probably confined to cases about which there could be uncertainty, or where it was desired to make an alteration. If we assume this, we may take the gafolgelda to be, as the word suggests, one who holds land from a lord at a rent; and both he and the gebur can be included in the phrase in Alfred’s treaty with Guthrum, “the ceorl who occupies gafolland” (see p. 416).
Nowell’s transcript of Otho B. xi reads XXX, as does Quadripartitus. This seems a more likely figure, but both these sources have CXX in the next chapter.
